stories.title: From the Panama Canal to Drewryville
stories.t: Hugh lost his father young and was 21 when he married Pearl Morris in May 1926. By the spring of 1930 he was a soldier in Battery B, 2nd Coast Artillery, at Fort Sherman on the Atlantic side of the Panama Canal; he sailed home for discharge in December 1930. He then spent the rest of his life farming in Southampton County, at Newsoms in 1940 and at Drewryville from the 1950s, where he died in 1973, a retired farmer and a member of Barnes Methodist Church. His draft card of 1940 describes him as 5 ft 9 in, 170 lb, with a ruddy complexion and gray eyes.

stories.title: Motherless at fifteen months
stories.t: Effie's mother Narcissa died in childbirth on 5 Oct 1868, when Effie was 15 months old, and a baby sister May died a month later. In 1870 Effie, aged 2, was living in the household of William R. E. Tomlinson in Greensville County while her father ran a dry goods and grocery business; by 1880 she was back with him and his third wife at Hicksford. She married her first cousin, the widower W. D. Grizzard Jr., in 1888 and raised his son Solon along with her own children.

stories.title: From Sussex to Sebrell
stories.t: The family stones at Sebrell-Simmons Cemetery show that George Thomas and Martha F. (Lane) Morris had their son Thaddeus in Sussex County in 1876 and were in Southampton County by the time their later children were born (Benjamin Franklin in 1881, Mudie in 1887, Edith in 1888). The family suffered a hard year in 1911: their daughter Mudie died in August at 24, and her sister Mary died five weeks later at 18. Two of the sons married sisters: Thaddeus married Mattie M. Gray in 1893, and Benjamin Franklin married her younger sister Lily Mary Gray in 1899, both daughters of Byrd Sugar Gray and Martha Ann Missouri (Beale) Bryant Gray.
stories.s: SCHS Cemetery Project, Misc. Vol. IV, Sebrell-Simmons Cemetery, Sebrell, plots 13, 14 and 14A (pp. IV-4 and IV-5): http://files.usgwarchives.net/va/southampton/cemeteries/miscvol4.txt (read via Wayback Machine copy; live server timed out); SCHS Cemetery Project, Riverside Cemetery, Courtland (RS-I-1, RS-I-23): http://files.usgwarchives.net/va/southampton/cemeteries/riverside.txt (read via Wayback Machine copy; live server timed out)

stories.title: From Newsoms to Chattanooga
stories.t: Lula Belle Vick grew up at Newsoms, the daughter of James Baker and Darthulia Worrell Vick, and married James Ashton "Buddy" Babb in 1914. Widowed at 49 when he died of pneumonia at Sebrell in December 1937, she was for many years a member of Newsoms Baptist Church. Late in life she moved to Chattanooga, Tennessee, to the home of her daughter, Mrs. Vann Hammel, and died there at Erlanger Hospital on 17 Mar 1960. She was brought home and buried with her parents in Hollywood Cemetery, Newsoms.
stories.s: Lula Vick Babb obituary, Tidewater News 21 Mar 1960 p.5, transcribed USGenWeb: http://files.usgwarchives.net/va/southampton/obits/b100l1ob.txt (read via Wayback Machine copy; live server timed out)

No link to John Vick or James Baker Vick was found

stories.title: Heavy artillery at Drewry's Bluff
stories.t: Warren David Braswell enlisted on 1 Mar 1862 at Brunswick in Capt. James H. M. Neblett's company of heavy artillery, raised from men of the 96th Virginia Militia and later commanded by Capt. Wiley G. Coleman. He signed for his clothing "his mark," so he probably could not write. In October 1864 his company was at Fort Drewry on Drewry's Bluff, guarding the James River below Richmond, and he was present on every roll from September 1864 to February 1865. In April 1865 he was paroled at Lynchburg as one of the men surrendered by Gen. Robert E. Lee. He went home to Brunswick County, where he and his wife Margaret raised a large family, and he died on 23 Sep 1911. In 1934 his son R. E. Braswell applied for the government headstone that marks his grave in the family cemetery.

stories.title: Nat Turner's rebellion, 1831
stories.t: In August 1831 Caswell Worrell was the overseer on Jacob Williams's farm in Southampton County. About 11 in the morning on 22 Aug 1831 Nat Turner's band reached the Williams place and killed Mrs. Williams, three of her children, a visitor named Edwin Drewry, and "the wife of the overseer, Mrs. Caswell Worrell," with her child (one list says two children). Caswell was away supervising work in a field and survived. On 3 Sep 1831 he testified for the prosecution at the trial of Nelson, one of the Williams slaves, saying that on the Thursday before the uprising Nelson had told him "they might look out and take care of themselves, that something would happen before long." Nelson was convicted and sentenced to hang on 9 Sep 1831. Seven months later, on 20 Mar 1832, Caswell married Jane Newsom; his bond named his mother Rhoda Worrell, which suggests he was still under 21. That Darthulia's father, named Caswell Worrell (mother Mary Drake, child born 1861), is this same man is probable but not proven: no second Caswell has been found in Southampton.
stories.s: Henry Irving Tragle, comp., The Southampton Slave Revolt of 1831: A Compilation of Source Material (Amherst, 1971): chronology p. xvii; Southampton County Court minutes, trial of Nelson (slave of Jacob Williams), 3 Sep 1831; trial table; and contemporary newspaper casualty lists. Full text: https://archive.org/details/southamptonslaverevolt1831

stories.title: An oath to the new republic
stories.t: Ambrose Grizzard married Lucy, daughter of John Fort, by January 1753, when her father's will called her "Lucy Grizzard." The family lived in what became Sussex County, where an Ambrose Grizzard stood godparent at Albemarle Parish baptisms again and again from 1767 to 1775. In 1777, during the Revolution, he took the Oath of Allegiance to the Commonwealth of Virginia in Sussex, the service for which the Daughters of the American Revolution recognize him as a patriot (ancestor A048776). He died before 16 Aug 1781. When his daughter Mary married Benjamin Baird in 1785, her bond called her "dau. Ambrose Grizzard, deceased."

stories.title: A soldier who never came home
stories.t: Joshua Wade, a Southampton farmer, married Elizabeth Brister (Bristow) in January 1855; their children included Rosa (born 1858) and Theophilus (born 1860). On 23 Apr 1862 he enlisted for the war at Craney Island in Co. B, 9th Virginia Infantry. Within days he was sick at the entrenched camp near Norfolk, and on 5 May 1862 he was sent to Richmond, where the May-June muster roll still listed him sick. Later rolls say he was furloughed home and "not heard from since." In February 1863 his company wrote that, "from information rec'd," he was "supposed to be dead." A Southampton veterans list dates his death 26 Jul 1862. He left a widow and small children.

stories.title: A widow's long pension fight
stories.t: His widow Rebecca swore in 1855 (aged 63) that Frederick was drafted in Sussex about 1 Sep 1814, served at Norfolk, and died in Sussex on 6 Feb 1850; she had already received an 80-acre bounty land warrant under the 1850 act. In 1872, aged 81, she applied for a widow's pension, giving her post office as Hicksford, Greensville Co., and saying he served at Craney Island and Norfolk in Capt. Isaac Mitchell's company and saw no active campaign. The pension was rejected on 10 Aug 1877 because she could not prove the marriage (29 Mar 1811, Northampton Co., N.C., by John Binford, magistrate).
stories.s: R. N. Grant, 1672 Samuel Judkins... and His Descendants (rev. 31 May 2022), Text volume, pp. 2390-2445 (Frederick J. Judkins estate and pension; William Grizzard family) and pp. 2617-2630 (William Herbert Judkins of Greensville): verbatim transcriptions of census, marriage, death, probate, pension and postmaster records: https://archive.org/details/1672-samuel-judkins-text

facts.t: Named as an infant child ("Frederick Judkins") of Charles Judkins, who died intestate 6 Mar 1803, in the 1803 Sussex Co. chancery complaint for division of Charles's land; called "my Brother Frederick Jones Judkins" in the 1798 will of Charles Judkins Jr. (Sussex W.B. F/107)

stories.title: A planter on Spring Swamp
stories.t: Charles Judkins was still a boy when his father died in Surry in 1710. As a grown man he patented 375 acres in 1725 and 370 more in 1729 south of the Nottoway River on Spring Swamp. With his wife Sarah he had children baptized in Albemarle Parish between 1737 and 1748, among them Charles (1742) and a son named Gray, the maiden name of his grandmother Lydia, daughter of the Jamestown planter Thomas Gray. He served on a Surry jury in 1746, viewed and surveyed roads for the new county of Sussex in 1754, walked the parish bounds as a processioner in 1755 and 1759, and was a constable in 1756. He made his will on 6 Nov 1773, and it was proved in June 1774.

notes: Round 3. The step from the minor son named in the 1710 Surry will to the Sussex man who died in 1774 rests on name, place and age (Grant), not on a record that names both. This is the softest documented link in the Gray-Judkins chain. Round 4 review of the weak link (son of Charles d. 1710): no deed, processioning return, tax list, parish entry or estate record naming both men was found in the free transcriptions (Grant 2000 and 2022, Albemarle Parish Register, Nugent). The Surry County order books for 1718-1741, where a guardianship, coming-of-age or estate division would be, are missing (Grant). No other Charles Judkins of the right age appears in Grant's complete descendancy of Samuel Judkins. Rating stays PROBABLE (identity by name, place, age and continuity).

stories.title: The Ancient Planter's daughter
stories.t: Lydia Gray was a daughter of the Jamestown Ancient Planter Thomas Gray. She married Samuel Judkins (Judkin) and was named "Lidia," his wife and co-executor, in his will of 1671/2. Within months she was a widow with a young son, Charles. On 10 Sep 1672 she signed a prenuptial bond before marrying Lt. Thomas Pittman. She was dead by 4 Mar 1678/9, when Pittman recorded the goods held for her orphan son Charles Judkins. Her descent from Thomas Gray was later worked out from the way his 800-acre Gray's Creek tract passed to her heirs.

stories.title: An Ancient Planter of Jamestown
stories.t: Thomas Gray reached Virginia before Sir Thomas Dale left in 1616, which made him an "Ancient Planter." At the muster of 24 Jan 1624/5 he was head of a household on James Island with his wife Margrett, son William (3) and daughter Jone (6). In 1635 he patented 550 acres across the river from Jamestown on Rolfe's and Cross creeks, 100 of them due to him as an Ancient Planter, with headrights for his first wife Anis, his "now wife" Rebecca, his sons William and Thomas and five servants. By 1652 he held 800 acres at the head of what became Gray's Creek in Surry. He married four times; his wife Rebecca testified in 1626 in the Joan Wright witchcraft case. He was dead by 2 Nov 1658. His daughter Lydia married Samuel Judkins, which links him to Holly's Judkins line.

notes: Round 3. JAMESTOWN-ERA ANCESTOR (Ancient Planter: in Virginia before Sir Thomas Dale left in 1616). Holly's 9x great-grandfather by the Gray-Judkins chain. Boddie's claim that he arrived in 1608 aged 15 is unsourced. Round 7 verdict on his English origins: UNKNOWN. No primary record names his parents, birthplace, ship or arrival year. The evidence stops at three points: he was in Virginia by spring 1616 (his 1635 patent), he is first named on 16 Feb 1623/4 at James City, and he was born about 1593/4 (from his deposition age, probable). The ship Starr, the 1608 arrival and every set of English parents found online are hypotheses; the Howick (Northumberland) parentage is contradicted. The one English record that might fit is the 1611 London marriage of Thomas Gray of Stepney, mariner, to Annes Vallentine (hypothesis). All existing ratings are unchanged.

stories.title: A German merchant's wife in Petersburg
stories.t: Rosa Blount Grizzard married Adolphus Herzog, a merchant born in Wuerttemberg, Germany, on 26 Aug 1863. He had enlisted as a private in Co. E, 16th Virginia Infantry, at Suffolk on 27 Apr 1861 and was discharged 14 May 1862 on appointment as postmaster (he had been postmaster of Stony Creek Warehouse since 1859). By 1870 they lived in Petersburg, where he was a junk dealer. Their infant son died of "teething" in July 1873. Rosa died in childbirth on 4 Apr 1876, aged 34, with a stillborn daughter; her newborn son Charles W. died 16 days later and was buried in her grave in Blandford Cemetery. Adolphus died of a pistol shot on Halifax Street, Petersburg, on 13 Nov 1877.

stories.title: Land bought from the Nottoway Indians
stories.t: John Fort received 100 acres on the Three Creeks, south of the Nottoway River, as a gift from his father Elias Fort in 1738. In 1745 he bought 445 acres on Buckhorn Swamp from the Nottoway Indians, and he also held land in North Carolina on Swift Creek and Buffalo Swamp. With his wife Rebecca he was executor of William Page's will in Isle of Wight. His own will, dated 10 Jan 1753 and recorded that March in the new county of Southampton, provided for his sons Elias, John, Henry, Joshua and Arthur, his daughter Betty and his "daughter Lucy Grizzard," Holly's ancestor.
stories.s: B. A. Chapman Collection (Blackwater Regional Library, Smithfield), Surnames, Fort: typed abstracts of Isle of Wight, Surry and Southampton deeds and wills with book and page: https://archive.org/details/b.-a.-chapman-collection-surnames-fort
